templates.pattern:
Statement: Should India adopt a four-day work week?
Argument I: Yes, it will improve employee productivity and work-life balance.
Argument II: Yes, it will reduce operational costs for companies.
Argument III: No, it is unsuitable for service industries and manufacturing sectors that require continuous operations.
Which arguments are strong?
templates.explanation: Argument I is strong — productivity and work-life balance are well-supported benefits. Argument II is weak — reduced costs is a secondary and debatable claim. Argument III is strong — operational continuity in key sectors is a genuine practical concern. I and III are strong.

templates.pattern:
Statement: Should India impose a sugar tax on soft drinks?
Argument I: Yes, high sugar consumption leads to diabetes and obesity, imposing a burden on public health.
Argument II: No, it will hurt the beverage industry and cause job losses.
Argument III: Yes, revenue from the tax can fund public health programmes.
Which arguments are strong?
templates.explanation: Argument I is strong — public health harm is a direct and proven concern. Argument II is weak — industry protection is not a strong reason to ignore public health. Argument III is strong — using tax revenue for health is a solid policy rationale. I and III are strong.

templates.pattern:
Statement: Should India implement a national population policy to control its growing population?
Argument I: Yes, overpopulation puts pressure on resources, infrastructure and employment.
Argument II: No, population growth is already slowing down naturally due to education and urbanisation.
Argument III: Yes, a smaller population will improve per capita income and quality of life.
Which arguments are strong?
templates.explanation: Argument I is strong — resource pressure is a direct and documented concern. Argument II is strong — natural demographic transition is a valid counter-argument. Argument III is weak — it is an oversimplification; per capita income depends on many factors beyond population size. I and II are strong.

templates.pattern:
Statement: Should criminals be allowed to contest elections?
Argument I: No, it corrupts the democratic process and brings criminals into positions of power.
Argument II: Yes, every citizen has the fundamental right to contest elections.
Argument III: No, elected representatives should be role models for society.
Which arguments are strong?
templates.explanation: Argument I is strong — democracy being corrupted by criminals is a direct, serious concern. Argument II is strong — fundamental rights cannot be curtailed without due process. Argument III is weak — role model reasoning is vague and subjective. I and II are strong.

templates.pattern:
Statement: Should the Right to Information Act be extended to political parties?
Argument I: Yes, political parties use public funds and should be accountable to citizens.
Argument II: No, it will expose internal party communications and hamper functioning.
Argument III: Yes, transparency in political funding will reduce corruption.
Which arguments are strong?
templates.explanation: Argument I is strong — accountability for public fund usage is a core RTI principle. Argument II is weak — internal communication concerns can be managed with exemptions; this doesn't override accountability. Argument III is strong — transparency reducing corruption is a direct benefit. I and III are strong.

templates.pattern:
Statement: Should India abolish the Rajya Sabha?
Argument I: Yes, it delays legislation and adds to the cost of governance.
Argument II: No, it serves as a revising chamber and prevents hasty legislation.
Argument III: Yes, most states have abolished their upper houses.
Which arguments are strong?
templates.explanation: Argument I is strong — delays and costs are genuine efficiency concerns. Argument II is strong — preventing hasty legislation is a core function of a revising chamber. Argument III is weak — what other states do is not a strong reason for India's federal structure. I and II are strong.

templates.pattern:
Statement: Should India sign the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty (CTBT)?
Argument I: Yes, it will improve India's global image and reduce nuclear risk.
Argument II: No, signing CTBT will constrain India's nuclear deterrence capability.
Argument III: Yes, it sends a positive signal for global nuclear disarmament.
Which arguments are strong?
templates.explanation: Argument I is weak — improved image is a secondary benefit. Argument II is strong — nuclear deterrence is a core national security concern. Argument III is strong — global disarmament is a legitimate strategic rationale. II and III are strong.

templates.pattern:
Statement: Should government schools be privatised to improve quality?
Argument I: Yes, private management leads to better accountability and efficiency.
Argument II: No, privatisation will make education unaffordable for the poor.
Argument III: Yes, competition among schools will improve overall standards.
Which arguments are strong?
templates.explanation: Argument I is weak — private management improving quality is not universally proven. Argument II is strong — unaffordability for the poor is a direct and serious consequence. Argument III is weak — competition improving standards is theoretical and not proven in school contexts. Only II is strong.

templates.pattern:
Statement: Should India build more highways through forest areas for economic development?
Argument I: Yes, better connectivity brings economic development to remote areas.
Argument II: No, deforestation and habitat destruction pose severe environmental risks.
Argument III: Yes, it will reduce travel time and boost trade.
Which arguments are strong?
templates.explanation: Argument I is strong — economic development of remote areas is a genuine public benefit. Argument II is strong — environmental destruction is a serious, proven concern. Argument III is weak — reduced travel time and trade boost are secondary benefits covered under I. I and II are strong.

templates.pattern:
Statement: Should India ratify the International Labour Organization's conventions on workers' rights?
Argument I: Yes, it will improve working conditions and wages for millions of workers.
Argument II: No, it may create inflexible labour laws that deter investment.
Argument III: Yes, it aligns India with global standards and improves its international standing.
Which arguments are strong?
templates.explanation: Argument I is strong — worker welfare is a direct and serious social benefit. Argument II is strong — investment deterrence is a genuine economic concern. Argument III is weak — international standing is a secondary benefit, not a strong reason. I and II are strong.

templates.pattern:
Statement: Should India adopt English as its official national language?
Argument I: Yes, English is a global language and its adoption will boost India's international competitiveness.
Argument II: No, it will marginalise speakers of Hindi and regional languages.
Argument III: Yes, it will create a uniform medium for administration across states.
Which arguments are strong?
templates.explanation: Argument I is weak — international competitiveness doesn't require English as official language. Argument II is strong — marginalising hundreds of millions of non-English speakers is a serious concern. Argument III is weak — Hindi or other Indian languages could also serve this purpose. Only II is strong.

templates.pattern:
Statement: Should India build a wall along its entire border with Bangladesh?
Argument I: Yes, it will stop illegal immigration and cross-border smuggling.
Argument II: No, it is impractical due to rivers and difficult terrain along much of the border.
Argument III: Yes, it will improve national security and prevent infiltration.
Which arguments are strong?
templates.explanation: Argument I is strong — stopping illegal immigration and smuggling is a direct security and law enforcement concern. Argument II is strong — physical and geographical impracticality is a real constraint. Argument III is weak — it largely repeats Argument I. I and II are strong.
